issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a rape trauma profile, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the only item that implies perpetration or morally troubling behaviour by the patient. Paired with memory items centered on terror and shame and trigger items tied to tiredness, driving with others, and sounds, this appraisal is hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type. The other negative appraisals reflect mistrust and loss of faith, which fit sexual assault trauma; this item instead points toward a different moral injury formulation and creates an internal mismatch within the Negative Appraisals node.

vignette: Elias Vance had driven the number forty-two route for twenty years before the summer layover fractured his routine. After fourteen hours of navigating gridlock, he had pulled into the abandoned transfer point, his body aching with a bone-deep exhaustion that made his hands tremble on the wheel. He had never expected vulnerability to find him in a place he considered neutral, but when the depot gate clanged shut, the sharp metallic echo trapped him before he could react. The violation was sudden and absolute. What frightened him most was the immediate dawning conviction that people could not be trusted and that he had lost his faith in any higher power to intervene. Over the following months, his mind began to hoard the assault like a damaged reel. He told his wife it played like a broken film, forcing him to sit in the dark until the terror he felt at the time fully collapsed into a profound shame that made him feel permanently marked. The fatigue that once signaled a routine shift now acted as a direct gateway to his trauma. When Elias pushed through his final stops, his eyelids growing heavy, that familiar exhaustion would immediately pull the assault into focus. He would find himself gripping the steering wheel until his knuckles whitened, the physical tiredness instantly unlocking the vivid, unspooled replay of the attack. The moment his body registered weariness, his mind could not help but drag him back to the exact second the hands had closed over him, turning a simple commute into a recurring reenactment. That same exhaustion, combined with the weight of carrying passengers, quickly solidified his growing conviction that the world was fundamentally broken. When he was forced to drive with others during crowded rush hour, the proximity of strangers immediately sharpened his belief that people could not be trusted. He stopped making eye contact, interpreting their glances through the lens of his own diminished worth. The daily reality of the bus route stopped being a job and became a continuous test of his suspicion; every distant siren and every tired passenger reinforced his certainty that he had lost his faith in life and in his own safety among them. His deepening suspicion did not just shape his daily interactions; it actively dictated how his past resurfaced. Because he had come to believe that he could not rely on anyone, his mind began to curate his flashbacks with ruthless severity. Every time the film of the assault rolled to its climax, his negative appraisal of the world flooded in, amplifying the intense shame he felt when recalling the event. He stopped fighting the memories, convinced that his body had been permanently defiled. The appraisal of universal untrustworthiness acted as a lens, turning neutral recollections into relentless confirmations of his own bodily disgrace. This entrenched pessimism did not stay confined to his thoughts; it actively recruited his environment into his suffering. His conviction that people were inherently dangerous made the mere presence of other commuters feel like an active threat. He began taking longer, darker routes to avoid shared stops, his mistrust transforming routine transit into a landscape of potential ambush. When the depot's security cameras buzzed or the brake hydraulics hissed, his belief that he had lost his faith left him feeling utterly exposed, stripping away any buffer against the noise. His negative worldview did not just coexist with his triggers; it sharpened them, ensuring that every sound and every ache would instantly signal impending danger. The cycle tightened when the memories themselves began to manufacture new points of entry. The unspooled film of the assault no longer waited for him to rest; it began to project its own demands onto his waking hours. When the replay brought back the same terror he felt at the time, his nervous system would hijack his routine, forcing him to abandon shifts the moment he felt even mildly fatigued. He could no longer tolerate driving with others, because the phantom weight of the attack would suddenly surface, making the driver's seat feel like a trap. The memory did not just return; it actively generated a new set of alarms, ensuring that fatigue and passenger proximity would forever be linked to the violation. Now, Elias sits in his small apartment, the radio quietly static, waiting for a clinician who might finally help him untangle the knot in his chest. He has not driven a city bus in eight months, and his wife, Claire, walks on eggshells around his sudden insomnia and the way he flinches at the hum of the refrigerator. He came to the intake hoping to reclaim some fragment of the man he was, but what frightens him most is the fear that the loop is permanent. He worries that if he ever steps back behind the wheel, or if his body simply gives out from exhaustion, the film will start again without warning.
